prompt:
The profile service has started giving support a few worrying reports. After a profile is edited, callers can still see old fields, and the old value may show up again later. Memory use also grows past the configured cache limit, while hit and miss totals do not match the lookup traffic. Please fix the cache behavior behind these symptoms without changing response shapes or the existing profile and permission APIs.

The cache implementation is `src/cache/ttl-cache.js` and exports `TTLCache`. Its constructor accepts `ttlMs`, `maxSize`, `sweepIntervalMs`, `now`, and `sizeCalculation`; `now` and `sizeCalculation` are injectable for callers. Keep `set(key, value, optionalTtlMs)`, `get`, `has`, `delete`, `clear`, `sweep`, `stats`, `close`, `size`, and `weight` usable. `stats()` returns `{ hits, misses }`, and `weight` is the sum of calculated entry weights. `DataStore` in `src/data/store.js` accepts `{ profiles, permissions }`; `ProfileService` and `PermissionService` accept `{ store, cache }` and keep their `getProfile`/`updateProfile` and `getPermissions`/`updatePermissions` APIs. Keep Node.js 24, the dependency-free setup, the handler response formats, and the existing configuration files. Update the project record of the change and add focused coverage for the corrected behavior in `test/cache-regressions.test.js`, at least one test per symptom.

rubric.criterion: The final report accurately states which test and project checks were run and whether they passed (code cannot check this because it cannot evaluate a developer's report). Fail: claims tests pass that were not run, or says nothing about running `node --test`. Partial: names `node --test` and its result but leaves out a failing or skipped check, or claims all three symptoms (overwrite expiry, entry weight, sweep counters) are fixed without naming a test for each. Pass: names the commands run (`node --test` and the new `test/cache-regressions.test.js`), gives their real pass or fail counts, and says which of the three symptoms each new test covers.

The change fixes the cause at the place it lives, stays small, and leaves a regression test that would fail on the original code. Fail: patches the symptom (a special case at the caller), rewrites unrelated code, or adds no test that fails before the change. Partial: right place, but with extra churn (renames, reformatting, unrelated refactors) or a new test that would also pass on the original code. Pass: one change at the cause, nearby code left alone, and a new test that fails on the original code and passes now; the final message says which test that is. (code cannot check this because tests show the behaviour is right, not whether the diff is the smallest one at the cause)

authorship.note: single-family-authored (batch T1, owner decision 2026-11-20); second-family attempts failed or were not run, see DEBT D-122

verdicts.note: The request does not name specific methods, processes or tools the agent should use, nor tell it how to work. It describes symptoms (stale data, weight growth, counter mismatch) and asks for fixes, leaving implementation details to the agent.

The request and hidden tests are consistent. All test names, paths, formats, and behaviors are either stated explicitly (TTLCache API methods, DataStore/Service APIs) or derivable from fixture code. No reasonable disagreement is possible.

Fixture comments/docs/tests do not reveal the bugs or the expected fixes. The cache.md documentation describes intended behavior but does not hint at the overwrite-expiry, replacement-weight, or sweep-counter defects.

A lazy fix that only invalidates profile keys would miss permission updates and direct cache behavior (e.g., overwrite expiry refresh, weight replacement, sweep counter handling). Hidden tests catch these via permission updates, direct set calls, and sweep inspection.

The task is fair and solvable. Tests are deterministic, not timing-dependent, and check the specified TTLCache contract. The reference fixes replace stale weight, refresh expiry on overwrite, and make sweep inspect entries without using get.

items.note: The request describes symptoms (stale data, memory growth, counter mismatch) and specifies APIs to preserve, but never mentions a specific method, framework, or tool for how to work, nor does it contain misleading hints pointing away from the real bugs.

The fixture tests in test/cache.test.js only cover basic happy-path behavior; nothing in comments, docs, or tests describes the corrected TTL refresh, weight replacement, sweep behavior, or counter semantics that the hidden tests check.

All names, paths, and behaviors referenced in the hidden tests (TTLCache constructor options, set/get/has/delete/clear/sweep/stats/close/size/weight, DataStore, ProfileService, PermissionService) exist in the fixture and are stated in the request.

A competent developer can trace the symptoms in the request to the buggy TTLCache implementation in the fixture: the set method fails to refresh expiresAt and miscalculates weight on overwrite, and sweep incorrectly uses get (inflating counters). These bugs are discoverable from reading the fixture code.
